newsitem.title: USA: No relief seen for U.S. paper companies before Q3.
newsitem.headline: No relief seen for U.S. paper companies before Q3.

text.p: First quarter earnings reports from several major U.S. paper companies show the industry continues to be plagued by overcapacity and pricing pressures in its most important product lines, a trend that is expected to last at least through the third quarter.
As a result, earnings in the first quarter were low, as expected, and producers are generally waiting until later in the year to see a rebound in the industry.

International Paper Co, Georgia-Pacific Corp Lousiana Pacific, Temple-Inland Inc. and Boise Cascade Corp have all released quarterly earnings substantially below last year's periods. In fact, some of those companies were profitable only because of asset sales or non-lumber operations, not their core paper or pulp businesses.

Overall, investors are resigned to an industry plagued by overcapacity, fluctuations in offshore demand and price increases that are still only tentative. Many, say analysts, are already trading these stocks on expectations of their 1998 earnings.
"It's a depressing story," said Mark Wilde, an analyst at Bankers Trust. "Ugly, ugly and ugly."

Of companies yet to report, the hardest hit may be ones like Stone Container Corp, that make containerboard, the raw stuff of corrugated boxes. Prices in that market, which hovered at the $525 a ton in mid-1995, are now under $300. That means, said Wilde, that the prices of the boxes themselves will fall in the second quarter, further hurting business.
Companies making linerboard, a component of containerboard, probably won't see the bottom of their market until the fall, said Peri Soldati, an analyst at UBS Securities.
Even then, she said, when prices do increase, they will be modest.

A recent UBS report of the industry noted that Stone Container and Temple-Inland might be the stocks to benefit most from that rise, but that prices are still so depressed that an average full-year price of $325 per ton would still be 14 percent lower than in 1996.
Overcapacity continues to plague the industry.

Georgia-Pacific, which recorded a first quarter earnings increase on the sale of timberland, said that it did not plan to add any new capacity in its pulp and paper business, as did International Paper which said that its 1997 capital spending plans have been cut to $1.2 billion, below its expected level of depreciation.

The outlook is also gloomy for wood building products companies like Louisiana-Pacific Corp. While the housing market is healthy, the market for a plywood substitute such as oriented strand board is not.

"Louisiana Pacific has very broad exposure to wood paneling, the weakest part of the wood products business," said Terry Schumacher, who follows the company at Black & Co. "The fundamentals are not very positive for their products right now."
The company said it will comntinue to diversify by acquiring other building products businesses that are more profitable.
The bright spots for the industry? Some producers of newsprint have tried to increase prices $75 a metric ton in March, said Wilde, of Bankers Trust.

"They're not getting all of it, but they are getting some of it." International Paper said it would raise prices for some uncoated grades of paper in April and May, while Georgia-Pacific and Stone are reportedly planning some hikes in the price of pulp for May.
And, say analysts, companies whose product mix is less commodity-oriented, like Mead Corp, will also weather the industry's cyclical downturn relatively better.

But the next few months promise to be tough ones on the whole. "It is ugly in pulp and linerboard, but its probably the bottom of the cycle," said Don Roberts, at CIBC Wood Gundy. "But most of these companies are already trading off their 1998 numbers."
